Teaching Process Dynamics and Control with a Digital Twin

From the tank equations to the lab bench: how a browser twin of the IT-5204 level trainer bridges theory and practice

Process dynamics is easy to write as equations and hard to feel. A first-order lag on a slide looks harmless. Watching a tank take four minutes to answer a pump change teaches more than any derivation.

In PIC-416 we use an IT-5204 level control trainer: a process tank, pump, solenoid and needle valves, an LVDT level sensor, and a control trainer with ON-OFF, P, PI and PID blocks. It is an excellent rig with one limit: one rig, many students, and a process whose time constant is minutes. So I built a browser-based digital twin of the trainer from the same equations students meet in class, and documented the whole setup. This article shows the model, the code that implements it, and how students move from theory to the bench with it.

1. The rig and its twin

Water is pumped into the tank and leaves by gravity through the solenoid valve (the main return path) and a needle valve that works as a load disturbance. Every controller signal is a 0 to 10 V voltage, so students handle the same signals as on the real trainer. The twin below is the actual file, running in your browser: choose a mode, press Acquire Data, and open the Graph and Wiring views.

2. Step one: model it

Students start with a signal chain, not with a transfer function. The LVDT and its interface turn level into volts. With gain and offset calibrated, 6 cm is 0 V and 14 cm is 10 V:

A volume balance on the tank is the central ODE (c = 1000/60 converts litres per minute to cm³/s; in the twin A = 555.6 cm², so c/A = 0.03 cm/s per LPM):

Water leaves through valves by Torricelli's law. The square root is the first source of nonlinearity: the more water, the faster it drains.

The solenoid valve and the pump are not instantaneous. Each gets a first-order lag, and the pump also has a static curve f(u) with a dead zone below about 1.5 V and saturation at 7.5 LPM:

Together these give a third-order nonlinear model in the states h, Q and σ:

The controller equations are just as compact. The integral is clamped, the output saturates at 0 to 10 V, and the derivative acts on a filtered measurement so a set-point change does not kick the output. For ON-OFF mode, H percent of the 10 V range gives the switching threshold:

3. Step two: from the nonlinear model to a transfer function

Linearising about a level h0 gives a tank time constant and gain that depend on where we operate. This is the lesson textbooks hide: G(s) is local.

The plant gain changes by more than 50 % and the time constant by about 100 s across the range. Students can check this on the twin by repeating a small open-loop step at two levels, and the linear model agrees with the nonlinear one for small steps:

The needle valve, the classic load disturbance, enters through its own first-order transfer function:

4. Step three: close the loop

With G(s) from above, each controller gives a different closed-loop polynomial. P control is fast but leaves an offset:

PI control removes the offset but raises the order and creates a stability limit on the integral gain:

With derivative on the measurement, PID gives a fourth-order characteristic polynomial. Students derive the coefficients on paper, then see the poles of the default settings:

a3tau_t tau_p + (tau_t + tau_p) tau_f
a2(tau_t + tau_p) + tau_f + K (Kp tau_f + Kd)
a11 + K (Kp + Ki tau_f)
a0K Ki

PD-1.431+0.418j , -0.143
PID-1.431+0.414j , -0.100 , -0.042

All poles are in the left half-plane, but the slow integrator pole near −0.04 explains why the level takes about 100 s to settle. ON-OFF control needs a different tool, the limit cycle. Ripple and period follow from the hysteresis band:

5. From equations to code

The point of a digital twin in a classroom is that the equations above are not hidden. The simulation core is a few lines of JavaScript, and students can read it next to the ODEs:

6. What students see

Open loop and nonlinearity. Below about 1.5 V the pump does nothing. Plant gain and time constant change with level. Students predict, measure and compare.

ON-OFF and hysteresis. The level cycles around the set value. Ripple and period grow with H, matching the formula within a pump-lag allowance:

P, PI, PID and the voltage inside the controller. A step to 50 % with Kp = 5, Ki = 0.15 and Kd = 5 shows the whole story in one plot:

ModeFinal PV (V)Offset (V)Overshoot (%)Settling (s)
P4.340.660.0not within ±2 %

PD4.340.660.0not within ±2 %
PID5.00-0.0019.4111
  • P stops 0.66 V short. The linear formula predicts only 0.13 V, because the pump dead zone and the nonlinear plant make the real offset larger.
  • PI removes the offset but overshoots by about 20 %, because the integrator keeps charging while the level is still rising.
  • PID: derivative changes the overshoot very little on a slow tank, but it multiplies the noise on the controller output several times over.

The Graph view splits the controller output into its three voltage contributions, Kp·e, Ki·∫e and −Kd·dy/dt. In steady state the integrator alone holds the voltage the pump needs, and the proportional term goes to zero. This is the clearest picture of what integral action means that I have found:

Students can also estimate Kp, Ki and Kd from their own logged data by least squares on MV = Kp·e + Ki·∫e − Kd·dy/dt, which links the identification theory to the controller they are tuning.

7. Wiring and the real trainer

Theory ends at a block diagram. A real trainer needs patch leads. The Wiring view redraws the trainer panel and lights up only the blocks and signal routes needed for the selected configuration, then lists the leads to connect. Changing from PID to ON-OFF moves the route from the PID block to the comparator:

Students predict on the twin, measure on the rig, and explain the difference. The twin is not a replacement for the lab: its parameters are reference values until students calibrate them against the rig, so calibration of the sensor, pump, outlet coefficient and tank area is part of the course. Measured data replace the model parameters, and the model earns its place by predicting a new test.

9. Outcomes, assessment and what to take away

Each experiment maps to course learning outcomes and programme outcomes, with a rubric: component and signal identification, calibration, model identification and validation, controller configuration and tuning, modern tool usage, and teamwork and reporting. The twin generates the evidence: logged data, exported tables and saved plots.

  • Show the equations and the code side by side. Students trust a model they can read.
  • Use the twin to predict, the rig to measure, and the gap to teach.
  • Let nonlinearity surprise them. The offset, the overshoot and the changing time constant are where understanding happens.
  • Be honest about limits: a twin is a model, and calibration is what makes it credible.

The repository has the technical documentation (P&ID, circuit blocks, ODEs, transfer functions, calibration), the OBE lab manual, the Python model and the twin. [Add your GitHub link here.] If you teach control or run a process lab, I would like to hear how you demonstrate dynamics.
